title: Instrument Maintenance & Calibration
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Science Laboratory Technology 300L curriculum: metrology fundamentals, calibration of common laboratory instruments (balances, pH meters, spectrophotometers, pipettes, thermometers, centrifuges), preventive maintenance, traceability, and calibration record-keeping.

questions.question: In metrology, what does 'traceability' of a measurement mean?
options: The measurement can be tracked by GPS
The measurement result can be related to a national or international reference standard through an unbroken chain of comparisons
The measurement was taken by a traceable analyst only
The measurement cannot be repeated
questions.correct_answer: The measurement result can be related to a national or international reference standard through an unbroken chain of comparisons
questions.explanation: Traceability means a measurement is linked, via a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations each with stated uncertainty, back to a recognized reference standard (e.g. SI units).

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between 'calibration' and 'verification' of an instrument?
options: They are exactly the same procedure
Calibration establishes the relationship between the instrument's readings and a reference standard, while verification confirms the instrument still meets specified performance criteria
Verification always changes the instrument's internal settings
Calibration is only done once in an instrument's lifetime
questions.correct_answer: Calibration establishes the relationship between the instrument's readings and a reference standard, while verification confirms the instrument still meets specified performance criteria
questions.explanation: Calibration compares/adjusts an instrument against a reference to establish its accuracy relationship; verification is a check confirming the instrument continues to perform within acceptable limits, without necessarily adjusting it.

questions.question: Analytical balance calibration weights are classified into accuracy classes (e.g. E1, E2, F1, F2, M1). Which class has the tightest (smallest) tolerance?
options: E1
F1
F2
M1
questions.correct_answer: E1
questions.explanation: OIML weight classes run from E1 (highest accuracy, smallest tolerance) through E2, F1, F2, M1, M2, M3 (progressively looser tolerances); E1 weights are used to calibrate the most precise balances.

questions.question: Before routine use each day, an analytical balance is typically checked using:
options: A certified reference check weight close to the expected working range
Only a visual inspection with no weight check
A random household object
The balance's maximum capacity weight only
questions.correct_answer: A certified reference check weight close to the expected working range
questions.explanation: A daily check weight near the routine working range confirms the balance reads correctly within its normal operating range before use.

questions.question: What does it mean if an analytical balance shows a consistent offset (bias) of +0.002 g across all reference weights tested?
options: The balance is perfectly calibrated
The balance has a systematic error that should be corrected/adjusted or the balance serviced
The balance should be discarded immediately with no further action
The reference weights are always wrong
questions.correct_answer: The balance has a systematic error that should be corrected/adjusted or the balance serviced
questions.explanation: A consistent offset across multiple reference weights indicates systematic bias, which should trigger adjustment/calibration or servicing rather than being ignored.

questions.question: A pH meter should be calibrated using how many buffer solutions at minimum for a reliable two-point calibration bracketing typical sample pH?
options: One buffer only
Two buffer solutions that bracket the expected sample pH range
Five buffer solutions always
No buffer is needed if the electrode is new
questions.correct_answer: Two buffer solutions that bracket the expected sample pH range
questions.explanation: A two-point calibration using two standard buffers (e.g. pH 4 and pH 7, or pH 7 and pH 10) that bracket the sample's expected pH establishes both the slope and offset of the electrode response.

questions.question: What does the 'slope' value reported after a pH meter calibration indicate?
options: The physical tilt angle of the meter
How closely the electrode's actual response to pH change matches the theoretical Nernstian response (~59.16 mV/pH at 25°C)
The battery charge remaining
The volume of buffer used
questions.correct_answer: How closely the electrode's actual response to pH change matches the theoretical Nernstian response (~59.16 mV/pH at 25°C)
questions.explanation: The slope compares the electrode's measured mV-per-pH-unit response to the ideal Nernstian value; a slope well below 100% (typically <90-95%) signals a worn or fouled electrode.

questions.question: Why must a pH electrode be stored in a storage/soaking solution rather than dry between uses?
options: Dry storage improves electrode response
Allowing the glass membrane and reference junction to dry out damages them and causes slow, unstable readings
It has no effect on performance
Dry storage is required by all manufacturers
questions.correct_answer: Allowing the glass membrane and reference junction to dry out damages them and causes slow, unstable readings
questions.explanation: The pH-sensitive glass membrane and reference junction must stay hydrated; drying out degrades the hydrated gel layer, causing sluggish, drifting, or inaccurate readings.

questions.question: In UV-Vis spectrophotometer calibration, wavelength accuracy is commonly verified using:
options: A holmium oxide or didymium filter with known characteristic absorption peaks
A random colored liquid
The instrument's power cable
A magnifying glass
questions.correct_answer: A holmium oxide or didymium filter with known characteristic absorption peaks
questions.explanation: Holmium oxide (or didymium) filters have sharp, well-characterized absorption peaks at known wavelengths, allowing verification of a spectrophotometer's wavelength accuracy.

questions.question: What does a stray light check on a spectrophotometer assess?
options: Whether ambient room light is too bright for the operator
Unwanted light reaching the detector that did not pass through the sample at the selected wavelength, which can distort absorbance readings
The color of the instrument's housing
The volume of the cuvette
questions.correct_answer: Unwanted light reaching the detector that did not pass through the sample at the selected wavelength, which can distort absorbance readings
questions.explanation: Stray light is radiation reaching the detector outside the intended wavelength band; excessive stray light causes non-linearity and inaccurate absorbance readings, especially at high absorbance.

questions.question: Photometric (absorbance) accuracy of a spectrophotometer is typically verified using:
options: Certified neutral density or standard absorbance filters/solutions of known absorbance
The instrument's user manual cover
A blank cuvette filled with air only, with no reference standard
Room temperature readings
questions.correct_answer: Certified neutral density or standard absorbance filters/solutions of known absorbance
questions.explanation: Certified absorbance standards (filters or solutions) with known absorbance values are measured to confirm the instrument's photometric accuracy against the certified value.

questions.question: The gravimetric method for calibrating a micropipette involves:
options: Weighing multiple dispensed volumes of distilled water on an analytical balance and converting mass to volume using water's known density
Measuring the pipette's length with a ruler
Timing how fast the pipette is used
Comparing pipette color to a reference chart
questions.correct_answer: Weighing multiple dispensed volumes of distilled water on an analytical balance and converting mass to volume using water's known density
questions.explanation: Gravimetric pipette calibration dispenses water repeatedly, weighs each dispensed amount on a calibrated analytical balance, and converts mass to volume using water's density at the measured temperature.

questions.question: In pipette calibration, what do the terms 'accuracy' (systematic error) and 'precision' (random error, %CV) of the pipette each describe?
options: Accuracy describes closeness of the mean dispensed volume to the nominal volume; precision describes the spread (reproducibility) among repeated dispenses
They are identical measures with no distinction
Accuracy only applies to balances, not pipettes
Precision measures color accuracy of the tip
questions.correct_answer: Accuracy describes closeness of the mean dispensed volume to the nominal volume; precision describes the spread (reproducibility) among repeated dispenses
questions.explanation: Pipette accuracy is how close the average delivered volume is to the set (nominal) volume; precision (often expressed as %CV) is how consistent repeated deliveries are with each other.

questions.question: A digital thermometer used for critical temperature monitoring (e.g. incubator, refrigerator) should be calibrated against:
options: A certified reference thermometer traceable to a national standard, at multiple points across its working range
Guesswork based on how the room feels
Only the manufacturer's claimed accuracy with no independent check
A thermometer of unknown calibration status
questions.correct_answer: A certified reference thermometer traceable to a national standard, at multiple points across its working range
questions.explanation: Calibrating against a traceable certified reference thermometer at points spanning the working range confirms accuracy across the temperatures the instrument will actually be used at.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach when volumetric glassware (e.g. a volumetric flask) needs calibration verification?
options: Gravimetric calibration: weigh the water it holds/delivers at a known temperature and convert to volume using water density
Estimate the volume by eye only
Assume all glassware from the same manufacturer is identical with no check needed
Measure only the external dimensions of the glass
questions.correct_answer: Gravimetric calibration: weigh the water it holds/delivers at a known temperature and convert to volume using water density
questions.explanation: Like pipettes, volumetric glassware accuracy is verified gravimetrically -- weighing the water contained/delivered at a known temperature and converting to volume via water's density.

questions.question: Why is water temperature recorded during gravimetric volumetric calibration?
options: It has no bearing on the result
Water density varies with temperature, so temperature is needed to accurately convert the weighed mass into a calibrated volume
It is only recorded for aesthetic completeness of the log
Temperature only matters for gas measurements
questions.correct_answer: Water density varies with temperature, so temperature is needed to accurately convert the weighed mass into a calibrated volume
questions.explanation: Water's density changes measurably with temperature, so an accurate mass-to-volume conversion in gravimetric calibration requires the measured water temperature.

questions.question: A centrifuge's rotational speed (RPM) is periodically verified using:
options: A calibrated tachometer
A stopwatch measuring color change
A pH meter
A UV-Vis spectrophotometer
questions.correct_answer: A calibrated tachometer
questions.explanation: A tachometer directly measures rotational speed and is used to confirm that a centrifuge's displayed RPM matches its actual rotor speed.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a preventive maintenance (PM) schedule for laboratory instruments?
options: To fix instruments only after they completely fail
To perform planned, routine inspection, cleaning, and servicing that reduces unexpected breakdowns and maintains performance
To avoid ever calibrating the instrument
To increase instrument downtime deliberately
questions.correct_answer: To perform planned, routine inspection, cleaning, and servicing that reduces unexpected breakdowns and maintains performance
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance proactively inspects, cleans, and services equipment on a schedule to catch developing problems early and reduce unplanned failures.

questions.question: What should be recorded in an instrument's maintenance/calibration logbook after every service or calibration event?
options: Nothing needs to be recorded
Date, technician/analyst identity, work performed, results/values obtained, and next due date
Only the technician's favorite color
Just a checkmark with no other detail
questions.correct_answer: Date, technician/analyst identity, work performed, results/values obtained, and next due date
questions.explanation: A complete calibration/maintenance record must show who did what, when, with what results, and when the next action is due, to maintain traceability and audit readiness.

questions.question: If a routine calibration check shows an instrument reading is outside acceptable tolerance ('out of tolerance'), the correct next step is to:
options: Continue using it for reporting results and ignore the finding
Take the instrument out of service, investigate/repair or adjust it, and assess the impact on any results generated since the last successful calibration
Delete the calibration record so it is not noticed
Increase the tolerance limits to make the reading pass
questions.correct_answer: Take the instrument out of service, investigate/repair or adjust it, and assess the impact on any results generated since the last successful calibration
questions.explanation: An out-of-tolerance finding requires quarantining the instrument, investigating/correcting the cause, and reviewing results reported since the last good calibration for potential impact.

questions.question: What is 'drift' in the context of instrument performance over time?
options: A sudden, one-time catastrophic failure
A gradual, progressive change in an instrument's readings away from the true value over time
The physical movement of the instrument on a bench
A software update
questions.correct_answer: A gradual, progressive change in an instrument's readings away from the true value over time
questions.explanation: Drift describes a slow, cumulative deviation of instrument response from the correct value, often due to component aging, fouling, or environmental effects, requiring periodic recalibration.

questions.question: Control charts (e.g. Levey-Jennings charts) used with periodic reference-material checks help a laboratory to:
options: Decorate the quality manual
Detect trends, shifts, or drift in instrument/method performance over time before results fall outside acceptable limits
Replace the need for calibration entirely
Calculate staff salaries
questions.correct_answer: Detect trends, shifts, or drift in instrument/method performance over time before results fall outside acceptable limits
questions.explanation: Control charts plot control-sample results over time so a technologist can visually spot trends or shifts indicating developing instrument problems before they cause reportable errors.

questions.question: What is 'linearity' as a calibration performance characteristic of an instrument such as a spectrophotometer?
options: The instrument's physical shape
The degree to which the instrument's response is directly proportional to analyte concentration across its working range
The straightness of the power cable
How quickly the instrument powers on
questions.correct_answer: The degree to which the instrument's response is directly proportional to analyte concentration across its working range
questions.explanation: Linearity describes how well instrument response (e.g. absorbance) tracks proportionally with concentration over the stated working range, usually assessed via a multi-point calibration curve and correlation coefficient.

questions.question: How often should a critical analytical instrument typically be recalibrated by an accredited external provider, in general laboratory practice?
options: Never, once installed
At a defined interval (e.g. annually, or per manufacturer/risk-based schedule) based on stability, usage, and risk, then verified in between
Every hour regardless of use
Only when it physically breaks down
questions.correct_answer: At a defined interval (e.g. annually, or per manufacturer/risk-based schedule) based on stability, usage, and risk, then verified in between
questions.explanation: Calibration intervals are set based on instrument stability, usage frequency, manufacturer recommendation, and risk, with routine verification checks performed between full calibrations.

questions.question: What information should a valid calibration certificate include?
options: Only the instrument's purchase price
Reference standard used, measured values with uncertainty, date, conditions, and traceability statement
The technician's personal phone number only
Nothing beyond a pass/fail stamp
questions.correct_answer: Reference standard used, measured values with uncertainty, date, conditions, and traceability statement
questions.explanation: A proper calibration certificate documents the reference standards used, results with measurement uncertainty, environmental conditions, date, and a statement of traceability so the calibration can be audited.

questions.question: What does 'measurement uncertainty' express about a calibration result?
options: The exact true value with no doubt
A quantified range within which the true value is believed to lie, with a stated level of confidence
The instrument's brand name
The cost of the calibration service
questions.correct_answer: A quantified range within which the true value is believed to lie, with a stated level of confidence
questions.explanation: Measurement uncertainty is a numerical estimate of the doubt about a measured value, expressed as a range around the result with an associated confidence level.

questions.question: Why should the base International System of Units (SI) matter to a laboratory technologist performing calibration?
options: It is irrelevant to laboratory work
Reference standards and traceability chains are ultimately linked back to SI base units (e.g. kilogram, metre, kelvin) to ensure global comparability of measurements
SI units apply only outside the laboratory
SI units were abolished
questions.correct_answer: Reference standards and traceability chains are ultimately linked back to SI base units (e.g. kilogram, metre, kelvin) to ensure global comparability of measurements
questions.explanation: Metrological traceability chains ultimately connect back to SI base units, which is what allows measurements made in different laboratories worldwide to be meaningfully compared.

questions.question: Autoclave performance qualification typically includes verifying that the chamber reaches and holds which condition to confirm effective sterilization?
options: 121°C at 15 psi for the validated holding time, confirmed with a biological or chemical indicator
Room temperature for 5 minutes
0°C for 1 hour
Any temperature above 40°C
questions.correct_answer: 121°C at 15 psi for the validated holding time, confirmed with a biological or chemical indicator
questions.explanation: Standard autoclave sterilization validation confirms the chamber reaches 121°C at 15 psi and holds it for the required time, verified using biological indicators (spore strips) or chemical indicators.

questions.question: Incubators and ovens used for critical temperature-dependent work should have their temperature uniformity checked by:
options: A single sensor placed in the center only, assumed representative of the whole chamber
Mapping temperature at multiple points throughout the chamber, since heating can be uneven
Never checking uniformity, only the set-point display
Checking uniformity only once at installation and never again
questions.correct_answer: Mapping temperature at multiple points throughout the chamber, since heating can be uneven
questions.explanation: Temperature mapping at several locations detects hot or cold spots caused by uneven air circulation, which a single central sensor reading would miss.

questions.question: When an instrument fault is suspected, what is the recommended first troubleshooting step before assuming a major component failure?
options: Immediately dismantle the instrument's internal circuitry
Check basic factors first: power supply, connections, consumables, recent calibration status, and error codes/manual troubleshooting guide
Discard the instrument and purchase a new one
Ignore the fault and continue reporting results
questions.correct_answer: Check basic factors first: power supply, connections, consumables, recent calibration status, and error codes/manual troubleshooting guide
questions.explanation: Systematic troubleshooting starts with the simplest, most common causes -- power, connections, consumables, and manufacturer guidance -- before assuming a major internal failure.

questions.question: Why should only manufacturer-approved spare parts and service technicians be used to maintain a critical analytical instrument where possible?
options: Approved parts and service preserve the instrument's calibration validity, warranty, and performance specifications
Non-approved parts are always cheaper and equally reliable
It has no bearing on performance or safety
Manufacturer parts are never available
questions.correct_answer: Approved parts and service preserve the instrument's calibration validity, warranty, and performance specifications
questions.explanation: Using unapproved parts or unqualified service can invalidate calibration, void warranty, and compromise the instrument's documented performance specifications.
